title: India's Top IT Firms Got 40 Per Cent Fewer H-1B Visas This Year. TCS Was Hit the Hardest.
excerpt: The $100,000 visa fee and a wage-weighted lottery are pushing the industry towards offshore work and local US hiring. The American dream is getting harder for 1.9 million IT employees.
body:
For the 1.9 million employees at India's six largest IT services companies, the path to America is narrowing fast. Official US data shows that H-1B visa approvals for TCS, Infosys, Cognizant, HCL Technologies, Wipro and Tech Mahindra fell 40 per cent in the fiscal year ending March 2026, dropping from 18,469 to 11,041.

The decline is not uniform. Tata Consultancy Services saw the steepest fall in the cohort, losing 3,242 approvals from the previous year to land at roughly 2,885. Infosys, by contrast, was the only firm in the group to gain ground, securing 3,195 approvals — the highest among the six.

## The $100,000 Wall

The Trump administration's September 2025 Presidential Proclamation requiring employers to pay $100,000 annually for every new H-1B worker has fundamentally changed the economics of sending engineers to the US. Combined with a wage-weighted selection process that now favours higher-paid applicants, the system has become a barrier to the entry-level, relatively lower-pay IT jobs that once formed the backbone of India's onsite delivery model.

"IT services companies are lowering their reliance on H-1B visas with the incremental $100,000 visa costs coupled with a wage-weighted selection process giving a preference to higher wage talent, thereby acting as a barrier to entry-level, relatively lower-pay IT jobs," said Sushovon Nayak, lead IT analyst at Anand Rathi Institutional Equities.



> **""What is likely to happen is that sub-contractor costs will increase as IT firms shift more people offshore, with most onshore work done by sub-cons," Nayak added."**


The result is a structural shift. Companies are moving more work offshore to India and relying on subcontractors for onshore delivery. "What is likely to happen is that sub-contractor costs will increase as IT firms shift more people offshore, with most onshore work done by sub-cons," Nayak added.


![Tata Consultancy Services — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/TCS_SIPCOT_Building.jpg/3840px-TCS_SIPCOT_Building.jpg)


## Industry Says It's Already Adapted

The firms themselves insist the numbers do not reflect a crisis. Cognizant CEO Ravi Kumar has said the company has "significantly reduced the dependency on visas, while increasing local hiring and our nearshore capacity." TCS chief K. Krithivasan said the firm had deployed "fewer people than the number of approvals each year" and that the decline was "part of a consistent reduction in dependency on visa-based talent over time."

But the USCIS itself is framing the decline as a policy success. "This data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over," the agency said in a post on X in late May, adding that the programme was now "better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers."

## A Broader Squeeze on Indian Workers

The H-1B crunch is one piece of a wider clampdown. In March, the Department of Labor proposed new rules mandating higher base wages for H-1B applicants. In October, Republican senator Tom Cotton introduced the Visa Cap Enforcement Bill to remove exemptions for colleges and non-profits from annual H-1B limits. And the HIRE Act, proposed by Ohio senator Bernie Moreno, would increase taxes on firms hiring offshore employees from their IT vendors.

Meanwhile, the green card pathway is also under strain. The US government's May 22 policy memorandum now requires foreign nationals applying for permanent residence to return to their home countries for consular processing, upending the lives of H-1B holders who have lived in the US for years. For Indians, whose green card backlogs stretch across decades, this is a particularly severe disruption.

At least five US lawmakers have criticised the new rule. "This radical policy will target people here LEGALLY, including people married to Americans and parents of US citizen children," said Arizona Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari.

For Indian IT professionals considering a move to the US, the arithmetic has changed. The $100,000 fee, the wage-weighted lottery, the offshore pivot, and the green card squeeze collectively signal that the era of mass H-1B deployments by Indian IT firms is over. The question now is whether the industry's shift to offshore delivery and local hiring will be enough to sustain growth — or whether the talent pipeline itself will start to fracture.
